question: Rare steak, reheated rice, mouldy cheese. Which of these kitchen fears are real risks, and which are overblown?
answer: Risk depends on where the germs can be. On a steak or a block of cheddar they stay on the surface, where heat or a knife reaches them. Mince, soft bread, raw flour and cooled rice hide them inside, or let them make toxins that cooking cannot undo. Looks tell you neither.
move: Ask where the danger sits before asking how bad it looks.
ask: Which food do I throw away out of fear, and which do I eat without a second thought?

items.note: Pink all the way through the middle.
items.verdict: Germs sit on the outside of a whole cut, and searing kills them.

items.note: Pink all the way through the middle.
items.verdict: Mincing spreads the surface germs all through. Cook it right through.

items.note: Cooked yesterday, left out overnight, microwaved.
items.verdict: Spores survive cooking, then make a toxin left out that reheating can't undo.

items.note: A spot of mould on a block of hard cheese.
items.verdict: Mould can't reach far into hard cheese. Cut 2.5 cm around the spot.

items.note: A spot of mould on one slice.
items.verdict: Its threads run through soft food unseen. Bin the loaf, not just the slice.

items.note: Raw off the spoon, made without eggs.
items.verdict: Raw flour has caused E. coli outbreaks. It is a raw crop, never heated.

items.note: Thawed in the fridge, then frozen again.
items.verdict: Safe if it stayed cold all along. It just comes out a little drier.
